Kysely adapter: store array fields as native Postgres arrays instead of jsonb

labels.name: database
labels.description: Database layer, all adapters, schema, migrations

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Summary

The Kysely adapter stores `string[]`/`number[]` fields as `jsonb` on PostgreSQL, while the Drizzle and Prisma generators use a native array column (`text[]`/`String[]`). The field works on every adapter, so this is a consistency follow-up rather than a bug: the goal is for the Kysely adapter to also use native Postgres arrays, so the physical schema matches across adapters and Kysely+pg users get native array capabilities (GIN indexing, array operators).

Surfaced by #9825, which added `account.grantedScopes: string[]`, the project's first array-typed field.

## Why it isn't a one-line flag flip

The Kysely adapter sets `supportsArrays: false` and stringifies arrays before writing ([kysely-adapter.ts#L842](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/d0390f5cdb73fee483b8033d8e474053ea72082c/packages/kysely-adapter/src/kysely-adapter.ts#L842)). Flipping it to be dialect-aware (`config?.type === "postgres"`, mirroring the adapter's existing `supportsJSON`/`supportsUUIDs`) and changing the generator's Postgres type from `jsonb` to `text[]` ([get-migration.ts#L425-L436](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/d0390f5cdb73fee483b8033d8e474053ea72082c/packages/better-auth/src/db/get-migration.ts#L425-L436)) is not sufficient.

Validated against real Postgres: the migration creates a `text[]` column, but the write path still sends a JSON string, and Postgres rejects it:

```
error: malformed array literal: "[\"test\"]"
```

Unlike Drizzle's ORM, the Kysely query-builder path does not format a JS array into a Postgres array literal (`{a,b}`). So the adapter needs explicit value-binding for native array columns, and the read path must return the driver's array as a JS array.

## Scope

- Teach the Kysely adapter to bind a JS array to a native Postgres array column and read it back, so `string[]`/`number[]` round-trip without stringification on Postgres.
- Make `supportsArrays` dialect-aware (native on Postgres, stringified JSON elsewhere), matching `supportsJSON`/`supportsUUIDs`.
- Change the generator's Postgres array type from `jsonb` to native (`text[]`/`integer[]`).
- Keep `matchType` accepting `jsonb` for back-compat so existing columns are not force-migrated.
- The e2e Postgres array suite must pass: [adapter.kysely.pg.test.ts](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/d0390f5cdb73fee483b8033d8e474053ea72082c/e2e/adapter/test/kysely-adapter/adapter.kysely.pg.test.ts) ("should support arrays").

## Migration consideration

Existing Kysely+Postgres deployments have `jsonb` columns. Because `matchType` accepts both, switching the generator to `text[]` will not auto-convert them, so this change should ship a deliberate `jsonb` to `text[]` conversion (or document the manual `ALTER`) to avoid old/new schema drift.

## Not a blocker for #9825

`grantedScopes` is functional on every adapter today and the Kysely adapter integration tests are green, so this is a deferred improvement, not a prerequisite.

items.body:
## Summary

Self-hosted deployments served over plain HTTP on a private network had no way to use `oauthProvider()`. Every `http` redirect URI on a non-loopback host was rejected, and the issuer was silently rewritten to `https`.

New option, off by default. It runs only when the default policy rejects an `http` URI:

```ts
oauthProvider({
  allowInsecureRedirectUri: (url) => url.origin === "http://192.168.1.50:8000",
});
```

The HTTPS rule moves out of the module-level Zod schemas, which cannot see plugin options, into one helper the plugin calls where it decides trust:

```diff
 registration / update   SafeUrlSchema -> syntax schema + policy (redirect_uris, post_logout_redirect_uris)
 /oauth2/authorize       SafeUrlSchema -> syntax schema + policy; failure shows the server error page
 authorize error redirect                 + policy (no error is redirected to a rejected URI)
 /oauth2/end-session     SafeUrlSchema -> syntax schema + policy
 /oauth2/token           SafeUrlSchema -> syntax schema only (must equal the code's redirect_uri, already checked)
 backchannel_logout_uri  unchanged
```

`SafeUrlSchema` in `@better-auth/core` keeps its behavior; it is now built from the exported `RedirectUriSyntaxSchema`.

Decisions a reviewer can't see in the diff:

- **A predicate, not a boolean.** Dynamic registration may be unauthenticated, so a global switch would let anyone register `http://anything`.
- **Not `validateRedirectUri`.** That hook decides matching and doesn't run at registration. Letting it override the scheme would give existing callbacks that never check the protocol the power to accept `http`.
- **One rule covers web clients on `localhost`.** "When the default rejects an `http` URI, the predicate decides" also lifts the web-client loopback ban, which is what #11445 asks for. Those callbacks need the predicate at authorize time too and match the registered port exactly; RFC 8252 port variance stays native-only, and native clients keep the exact loopback host rule.
- **The issuer gets no option.** Tokens already carry the configured issuer (`token.ts`, `introspect.ts`); only `getIssuer` rewrote it. The fix deletes the rewrite.

Closes #11277
Closes #11740
Closes #11445

The option shape comes from @ArjunCodess's work in #11342, credited as co-author.

## Evidence

New tests in `insecure-redirect-uri.test.ts` (10 fail with the fixes reverted; all 15 pass with them):

```text
registered http URI, no option   -> authorize redirects the error to http://192.168.1.50:8000   (before)
                                 -> /api/auth/error?error=invalid_request                        (after)
option allows LAN origin         -> registration rejected                                       (before)
                                 -> register, authorize, token exchange succeed                  (after)
web client http://localhost      -> rejected                                                    (before)
                                 -> accepted when the option allows it                           (after)
baseURL http://10.0.0.5:3000     -> discovery/iss https://..., id_token iss http://...           (before)
                                 -> all three http://10.0.0.5:3000/api/auth                      (after)
```

Also covered: a web client on `localhost` using a different port, a stored web `localhost` client without the predicate, `http://127.1` for native clients, credentials in a post-logout URI, and a logout confirmation after the predicate narrows. These pass both before and after: default registration rejection, origins the predicate doesn't allow, a throwing predicate, and a registered `http` post-logout URI without the option (400).

The dynamic baseURL e2e test asserted the old `https` rewrite; it now expects the configured `http` issuer.

The full oauth-provider, core, cimd, and mcp suites pass, as does `pnpm typecheck`.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way

**Blast Radius:** narrow

Without the option, redirect URI behavior is unchanged. The one output change: a deployment whose issuer is `http` on a non-loopback host now reports `http` in discovery and in the authorization response `iss` parameter. The ID tokens of those setups already carried `http`, so OpenID Connect validation was failing. The risky case is a TLS-terminating proxy where `baseURL` resolves to `http` and discovery showed `https` by accident. The changeset and docs tell those users to set `baseURL` to the public `https` URL.

items.body:
## Summary

The MCP plugin's OAuth implementation does not enforce PKCE for public clients by default, creating an authorization code interception vulnerability.

## Vulnerability Details

**Package:** `@better-auth/mcp` (packages/better-auth/src/plugins/mcp/)
**Severity:** Medium-High (CVSS ~6.8)

### Root Cause

The `requirePKCE` option in `OIDCOptions` (types.ts L101) has no default value. In the MCP plugin's option construction (index.ts L183-198), `requirePKCE` is absent from the defaults object. It only appears if the user explicitly passes it via `options.oidcConfig`.

By contrast, the oauth-provider package uses `isPKCERequired()` (utils/index.ts L658-681) which **always** enforces PKCE for:
- Public clients (type === "public", tokenEndpointAuthMethod === "none", etc.)
- Clients requesting offline_access scope
- Per-client `requirePKCE ?? true` (defaults to TRUE)

The MCP plugin does NOT use `isPKCERequired()`. It uses the simpler `opts.requirePKCE` boolean, which defaults to `undefined` (falsy).

### Exploit Scenario

1. A public client (type: "public") is registered via `/mcp/register`
2. Attacker initiates OAuth flow WITHOUT PKCE:
   GET /mcp/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=<public_client>&redirect_uri=https://attacker.com/cb&scope=openid
3. authorize.ts L139-150: Check `(!query.code_challenge || !query.code_challenge_method) && options.requirePKCE` — `requirePKCE` is undefined, so this is SKIPPED. No PKCE required.
4. Authorization code is issued and stored WITHOUT a code_challenge (authorize.ts L223-224 stores `codeChallenge: query.code_challenge` which is undefined)
5. If the authorization code is intercepted (via referrer headers, browser history, server logs, network interception), the attacker redeems it:
   POST /mcp/token with grant_type=authorization_code&code=<intercepted_code>&redirect_uri=https://attacker.com/cb&client_id=<public_client>&code_verifier=anything
6. Token handler L627-635: Public client check requires `code_verifier` — attacker provides arbitrary value
7. L672: `value.codeChallenge` is null/undefined (never stored) — check SKIPPED
8. L679: `value.codeChallenge` is null/undefined — PKCE verification SKIPPED entirely
9. Token is issued to the attacker

### Impact

For public clients (which cannot store a client_secret), PKCE is the **only** RFC 7636 mitigation against authorization code interception attacks. The MCP metadata advertises `code_challenge_methods_supported: ["S256"]` and `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported: ["none"]`, signaling public client + PKCE support — but PKCE is not enforced by default.

### Comparison: oauth-provider vs MCP Plugin

| Aspect | oauth-provider | MCP Plugin |
|--------|---------------|------------|
| PKCE required for public clients | Always (isPKCERequired L670) | Only if opts.requirePKCE (defaults to undefined) |
| PKCE required for offline_access | Always (L675) | Not checked |
| Per-client requirePKCE default | ?? true (L679) | N/A |
| isPKCERequired function used | Yes | No |

### Secondary Finding: oauth-provider plain PKCE broken at token endpoint

oauth-provider token.ts L835-838:
`challenge = code_challenge_method === "S256" ? generateCodeChallenge(code_verifier) : undefined`

If method is "plain", challenge = undefined, which will never match the stored code_challenge. Plain PKCE is accepted at the authorize endpoint (if allowPlainCodeChallengeMethod is enabled) but ALWAYS FAILS at the token endpoint. While `allowPlainCodeChallengeMethod` defaults to false, admins who explicitly enable it get a broken flow.

### Fix

Add `requirePKCE: true` to the MCP plugin's default opts:
`requirePKCE: true,` in the opts object at index.ts L183-198.

Additionally, implement client-type-aware PKCE enforcement matching oauth-provider's isPKCERequired behavior for public clients regardless of config.

items.title: Adapter types should respect supportsDates: false

labels.name: locked
labels.description: Locked conversations after being closed for 7 days

items.body:
## Problem

When an adapter sets `supportsDates: false` in its config, the runtime behavior correctly converts dates to/from the adapter's native format. However, the **TypeScript types** always use `Date` for date fields regardless of this setting.

This means adapters like Convex (which stores dates as numbers/milliseconds) have a type mismatch: TypeScript says `createdAt: Date` but the actual runtime value is a `number`.

## Current behavior

```typescript
const session = await auth.api.getSession({ headers });
// TypeScript thinks: session.createdAt is Date
// Runtime reality: session.createdAt is number (ms since epoch)
```

## Expected behavior

When `supportsDates: false`, date field types in API responses should reflect the adapter's actual output type, or there should be a mechanism for adapters to specify the output type for date fields.

## Context

This affects the [Convex adapter for better-auth](https://github.com/get-convex/better-auth). Convex doesn't support the `Date` type — it uses numbers for timestamps. Our adapter's `customTransformOutput` returns `new Date(data).getTime()` for date fields, but the types still say `Date`.

A contributor tried to "fix" the type mismatch by making the runtime return `Date` objects instead (to match the types), but this broke Convex serialization since `Date` isn't a supported Convex type. We had to revert that fix.

## Relevant code

In `@better-auth/core`, the type inference for date fields (`InferDBValueType<"date">`) always resolves to `Date`, with no conditional based on adapter config:

- `node_modules/@better-auth/core/dist/db/type.d.mts` — `InferDBFieldOutput` always returns `Date` for date fields
- `node_modules/@better-auth/core/dist/db/schema/session.d.mts` — hardcoded `ZodDate` types

## Possible solutions

1. Make `InferDBValueType` generic over adapter config so `supportsDates: false` changes the output type
2. Add a type-level hook (similar to `customTransformOutput`) that lets adapters specify their date output type
3. Add a generic type parameter to the adapter factory that maps field types

items.title: fix(phone-number): deduplicate verification records on repeated OTP requests

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: credentials
labels.description: Email/password, magic-link, OTP, phone, username, passkeys

labels.name: locked
labels.description: Locked conversations after being closed for 7 days

items.body:
## Summary

- **Root cause:** `createVerificationValue` inserts without dedup — when a user requests a second OTP before the first expires, duplicate verification records accumulate. Subsequent calls to `updateVerificationByIdentifier` or `deleteVerificationByIdentifier` then operate on multiple rows for the same identifier, causing 500 errors.
- **Fix:** Add a `createOrReplaceVerification` helper that deletes any existing verification for the identifier before creating a new one. Applied to all 3 `createVerificationValue` call sites in the phone-number plugin:
  - `signInPhoneNumber` (requireVerification flow)
  - `sendPhoneNumberOTP`
  - `requestPasswordResetPhoneNumber`

## Trade-offs

This fix adds an extra DELETE query per OTP send (n+1). In practice, OTP sends are low-frequency user-initiated actions, and the DELETE is a simple indexed lookup on `identifier` — so the DB load is negligible. The cost is primarily the extra network round-trip to the database.

### Single-statement alternatives (follow-up)

Since this helper centralizes the logic in one place, a follow-up could detect DB capabilities and use the optimal strategy per database:

1. **Upsert** — `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (identifier) DO UPDATE` (Postgres/SQLite) or `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` (MySQL). Single statement, atomic, no extra round-trip. Requires a unique constraint on `verification.identifier`.
2. **`REPLACE INTO`** (SQLite/MySQL) — atomic delete-then-insert in one statement. Also requires a unique constraint.
3. **Transaction** — wrap DELETE + INSERT in the adapter's `transaction()` method. Atomic, no unique constraint needed, still two statements but could be pipelined. The `DBAdapter` already exposes `transaction` support.

Options 1 and 2 are the cleanest but depend on adding `unique: true` to the `identifier` column in `get-tables.ts` — a breaking change for existing DBs that may already have duplicate records blocking the migration. Option 3 could work today by passing `ctx.context.adapter` into the helper for its transaction support.

If the n+1 is unacceptable for this PR, happy to pursue any of these here. Otherwise they make good follow-ups since the helper already centralizes the logic, making the swap straightforward.

## Test plan

- [x] Added test: repeated `sendOtp` calls produce exactly 1 verification record (not 3)
- [x] Added test: wrong code → re-send OTP → correct latest code succeeds
- [x] Added test: repeated `requestPasswordReset` calls produce exactly 1 verification record (not 2)
- [x] Added test: repeated password reset requests followed by reset succeeds
- [x] All 30 tests pass (4 new + 26 existing, zero regressions)
- [x] No type errors introduced
- [x] Lint clean

## Future improvements

- **Adapter-aware verification replacement** — `DBAdapter` exposes `id`, `options.adapterConfig.adapterId`, and `options.type`, which could be used to select the optimal dedup strategy per database (e.g., `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` for Postgres, `REPLACE INTO` for MySQL/SQLite, or `transaction()` as a universal fallback). This could be implemented as a `createOrReplaceVerificationValue` method on `InternalAdapter` that inspects the adapter config and dispatches accordingly.
- Add `unique: true` to `identifier` in `get-tables.ts` (breaking change for existing DBs with duplicates — should be bundled with a minor version bump). Users who want to add it early can do so safely after this fix lands, and `npx auth migrate` won't overwrite it.
- Fix the same latent bug in email-otp and other plugins

## Summary

- use a provider-aware lookup in the social link callback so matching is scoped by both `accountId` and `providerId`
- add a focused regression test that links Google and GitHub accounts sharing the same external id and asserts both linked rows are preserved

## Root Cause

The link callback was calling `findAccount(String(userInfo.id))`, which searches only by external account id. When two different providers return the same external id, the callback could update the wrong linked account row instead of creating or updating the provider-specific row.

## Impact

- prevents cross-provider account collisions during social account linking
- keeps provider-specific linked accounts intact when external ids overlap

## Validation

- `pnpm build`
- `pnpm --filter better-auth test --run src/api/routes/callback-link-account.test.ts`

items.title: feat(oauth-provider): add DPoP support

labels.name: locked
labels.description: Locked conversations after being closed for 7 days

items.body:
OAuth provider resource servers need a first-class DPoP path so sender-constrained tokens cannot be accepted through bearer-only verification.

This adds a shared DPoP proof verifier to the OAuth core and makes the resource-server boundary request-aware. `verifyAccessToken` is renamed `verifyBearerToken` to make its bearer-only contract explicit, and it now rejects DPoP-bound tokens. `verifyAccessTokenRequest` is the path that accepts them, because it has the request method, URL, authorization scheme, proof header, and access-token hash. A new `requestToResourceInput` helper maps a standard `Request` onto that contract, so every resource-server entry point reads the wire request the same way.

The provider binds issued access and refresh tokens to `cnf.jkt` when a client registers for DPoP, an authorization code carries `dpop_jkt`, or a protected resource requires DPoP-bound tokens. The binding is carried through refresh-token rotation, introspection, and userinfo, and enforced at every resource boundary. MCP advertises DPoP in protected resource metadata and verifies DPoP-bound requests through the same request-aware contract.

Proof replay reuses the existing single-use verification store rather than a dedicated table. Anti-replay therefore holds across instances wherever verification is database-backed.

Reviewer notes:
- Replay is backed by the verification reservation primitive through `createDpopReplayStore`, so there is no bespoke replay table. A deployment whose verification store is secondary-storage-only rejects DPoP requests instead of silently skipping replay protection.
- Server-issued DPoP nonce challenges are out of scope.

Fixes https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/issues/8656

items.title: feat(oauth-provider): Support pairwise subject identifiers (OIDC Core Section 8)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or improvement

labels.name: locked
labels.description: Locked conversations after being closed for 7 days

items.body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem?

The `@better-auth/oauth-provider` plugin documents awareness of pairwise subject identifiers in the `OIDCMetadata` type (`types/oauth.ts:206-213`):

```typescript
/**
 * Supported subject types.
 *
 * pairwise: the subject identifier is unique to the client
 * public: the subject identifier is unique to the server
 *
 * only `public` is supported.
 */
subject_types_supported: "public"[];
```

However, the implementation always uses `sub: user.id` directly — the same value for every relying party. Any two RPs that receive tokens for the same user see an identical `sub` and can trivially correlate users across services.

This is a compliance gap with [OIDC Core Section 8](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#SubjectIDTypes), which defines two subject identifier types:

- **public** (current behavior): same `sub` for all clients
- **pairwise**: `sub` is unique per client, preventing cross-RP linkability

Pairwise identifiers are required by privacy-preserving OIDC deployments (e.g., age verification under CNIL's "double anonymity" framework, eIDAS 2.0 wallet ecosystems) and are supported by all major OIDC providers (Keycloak, Auth0, Azure AD, Google).

## Describe the solution you'd like

### 1. Per-client `subject_type` field

Add `subject_type?: "public" | "pairwise"` to the `OAuthClient` interface and the `oauthClient` database schema. RPs set this during DCR or manual registration.

### 2. Pairwise `sub` computation

When a client has `subject_type: "pairwise"`, compute a pseudonymous identifier instead of using `user.id`:

```
sub = Base64URL(SHA-256(sectorIdentifier + "." + userId + "." + salt))
```

Per [OIDC Core Section 8.1](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#PairwiseAlg), `sectorIdentifier` is derived from the client's `sector_identifier_uri` (if registered) or the host component of the registered redirect URI. The `salt` is a server-side secret.

### 3. Fix `sub` placement in token construction

Currently, `sub: user.id` is placed _after_ the `customClaims` spread in both `createJwtAccessToken` (`token.ts:100`) and `createIdToken` (`token.ts:160`), meaning custom claims hooks cannot override `sub` either:

```typescript
// token.ts — createIdToken (line 154-166)
const payload: JWTPayload = {
  ...customClaims,
  ...userClaims,     // has sub: user.id
  auth_time, acr, iss,
  sub: user.id,      // hardcoded last → overwrites any custom sub
  aud, nonce, iat, exp,
};
```

The computed `sub` should be resolved before payload construction:

```typescript
const resolvedSub = client.subject_type === "pairwise"
  ? computePairwiseSub(user.id, client, serverSecret)
  : user.id;

const payload: JWTPayload = {
  ...customClaims,
  ...userClaims,
  sub: resolvedSub,
  // ...
};
```

This also applies to `userNormalClaims` (`userinfo.ts:26`) and introspection endpoints (`introspect.ts`).

### 4. Update discovery metadata

`metadata.ts:90` currently hardcodes `subject_types_supported: ["public"]`. When configured with a pairwise secret, advertise both:

```json
{ "subject_types_supported": ["public", "pairwise"] }
```

### 5. Plugin configuration

Add an optional `pairwiseSecret` to `OAuthOptions`:

```typescript
oauthProvider({
  pairwiseSecret: process.env.PAIRWISE_SECRET, // enables pairwise support
})
```

If not provided, pairwise client registrations should be rejected and discovery advertises only `["public"]`.

## Describe alternatives you've considered

- **Override `sub` via `customIdTokenClaims`**: Not possible — `sub: user.id` comes after `...customClaims` in the payload spread and overwrites it.
- **`pnpm patch` the spread order**: Works short-term but fragile across upgrades.
- **Deploy a separate OIDC proxy** (Keycloak, Hydra) for pairwise support: Adds operational complexity for a feature that belongs in the auth layer.

## Additional context

Relevant specs:

- [OIDC Core Section 8 — Subject Identifier Types](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#SubjectIDTypes)
- [OIDC Core Section 8.1 — Pairwise Identifier Algorithm](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#PairwiseAlg)
- [RFC 7591 Section 2 — `subject_type` in client metadata](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7591#section-2)

The codebase already acknowledges this gap (`types/oauth.ts:206-213` and `oidc-provider/types.ts:499-505`). The `OAuthClient` index signature (`[key: string]: unknown`) allows storing `subject_type` on clients today, but the runtime never reads it.

**Affected files:**

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `types/oauth.ts` | Add `subject_type` to `OAuthClient`, widen `subject_types_supported` type |
| `types/index.ts` | Add `subjectType` to `SchemaClient` and DB schema |
| `token.ts` | Compute pairwise `sub` in `createJwtAccessToken` and `createIdToken` |
| `userinfo.ts` | Use computed `sub` in `userNormalClaims` |
| `introspect.ts` | Use computed `sub` in introspection responses |
| `metadata.ts` | Conditionally advertise `["public", "pairwise"]` |
| `register.ts` | Accept and validate `subject_type` in DCR |

Happy to contribute a PR if this direction aligns with the project's roadmap.
